ch-01.beat_text: She accepts the commission without having settled what she owes him for raising and for craft. He does not offer to go in her place and does not speak the thing he has withheld. The hamlet treats the acceptance as the end of the meeting.
She leaves the forge-house for the village path with a pack the hamlet can spare, no mount, and no guide. Orren remains at the unfinished iron. The house holds only him.
Willa leaves the village path and climbs the winter pass on foot in the last weeks before midwinter. The path is open. She meets no holders of the pass and no mounted traffic. She does not turn back.

The crossing exacts cold and walking time she cannot spare. She spends stamina she will need for the return and for the work waiting at the forge. She keeps moving because a late arrival spends the retrieval.
After dark Willa finds the lee camp and comes down off the pass into its edge. She does not announce herself. She waits until the band is down to hungry rest and does not draw a weapon.
Willa recrosses the winter pass with the relic in the pack. The return takes longer than the ascent. She does not meet Orren on the path. She does not stop to open the piece.
Cold takes her hands. She wraps them and keeps walking, and the frost stays in the skin. She does not stop to thaw them properly, because a late return spends the retrieval.
No messenger from the house meets her on the return, and she does not meet Orren on the path. She spends her remaining strength on the recrossing. The hours go to walking, not to hearing him.

Willa reaches the forge-house in the evening with the pack still on. Orren is there. She does not sleep. She does not put the piece back in the village chest. The unfinished tithe-iron is still on the forge.

She reads Orren's weld in the join and an inclusion where a living levy sits. She does not take that reading to the hamlet or to the Hold. She keeps the piece in her own custody through the rest of the evening.

She does not sleep on the reading. The commission is finished in the only way the hamlet will count: the piece is in the house and the rite is still days off. She does not give the piece back to the chest.

She sets out the wrong weight, the forty-year weld, and the inclusion as facts of the metal, not as an accusation of the man. She treats the reading as work he is owed to hear first. She does not take the same reading to the village or name the Hold. The piece stays in her custody while she speaks.

She tries to name what she owes him for the raising, for the craft, and for the lie that kept the grain coming, and she cannot make the three debts add into one payable sum. He does not offer a figure that would clear them. The ledger stays open because no payment fits the time left.

Willa sets the terms of what she will and will not do, speaking them as a cut in the work rather than as a plea. She will not break the relic. She will not tell the Hold or the village. She will not keep the lie after he dies. He listens without interrupting the list.

She adds that she will work the winter because the hamlet cannot spare a smith, and that she will leave when the pass opens in spring. She does not ask him to approve the leaving. She does not withdraw it. He does not refuse the terms or treat them as a question.

On midwinter day Willa and Orren leave the forge-house with the relic in her pack and the thin tithe between them. The house stands empty behind them. They walk the short cold road to the midwinter ground. Her frosted hands stay ungloved on the straps so the steward can see the crossing.

The Hold's steward is already at the table with the year's book. Willa sets the village weight and the thin tithe on the board. She presents both as Highkettle's due. Orren stands a pace behind and does not speak for the house. No one of the hamlet has come to speak against the weight.

They walk the accepted pieces back from the midwinter ground and bring them into the forge-house. She sets the relic and the thin tithe on the house bench, not in the village chest. The house holds both of them again. Neither treats the return as a finished talk.

ch-02.beat_text: He does not deny forging the piece forty years ago. He does not deny binding the levy to himself so the compact would hold. He receives the weld as his own work and the inclusion as his own tax. He does not ask what she intends to do with the knowledge before he speaks of how it was made.

She has him hold a bar and watch the tremor he no longer hides. The years of the levy sit in the shake and in how long he needs before he can set the bar down. He does not claim the shake is only age or only work. The old necessity is visible as a body already spent.

They walk the accepted pieces back from the midwinter ground and bring them into the forge-house. She sets the relic and the thin tithe on the house bench, not in the village chest. The house holds both of them again. Neither treats the return as a finished talk.

He names the old reasons again: the slide year, and the village that could not have survived it. He does not ask to be forgiven. He does not add a new defense for the years since. She lets the old reasons stand as past and does not grant that they still hold.

In the morning they take up shared work without restoring the house that raised her. He goes to the fire as a man still paying the levy in his body. She takes the winter's smith-labor as already decided and does not unpack the leaving. Neither greets the other as master or child of the house.

lo-02.beat_text: She is the only traffic on the pass. Ahead the far-slope band is a party of hungry people, not an army. She rations sleep and fuel and judges each day's distance by the weight of the pack and the state of her feet.
She is the only traffic on the return. The pass is still open on foot. No Hold party meets her. She keeps the piece in the pack and does not show it to anyone on the way down.
The pass behind her holds no traffic now. She sets the recovered relic on the forge balance before she eats or sleeps. Her marked hands work the pan as they would for a bad heat.

lo-03.beat_text: Only after she is gone does the camp find the piece missing. Their rest breaks into the knowledge of the loss. They do not pursue into the dark in any force she can hear.

lo-04.beat_text: They do not go on to the forge for the year's iron, being unable to carry both. The village chest is left empty. They turn back toward the winter pass with only the piece.

lo-05.beat_text: The steward weighs the tithe by the board-mark and turns the relic once in the light. The steward does not cut, does not sound the weld, and does not test the inclusion. No public challenge is spoken. The steward accepts both objects as sufficient for the year and marks the book.

ob-01.beat_text: They lift the presentation-relic from the chest and take it because they can carry one object and because their own slopes have no Hold protection and they are hungry. They do not linger to weigh it.
She lifts the piece and withdraws. She kills no one for a village object. She leaves them the rest of what they have. The camp does not raise a watch in time to stop her.

ob-02.beat_text: They go back to the unfinished tithe and work it through the day. They draw the bars to the weight the remaining stock will bear and no more. The iron comes out thin and honest to the shortage. Neither of them adds scrap they do not have to fake a fuller levy.

ob-03.beat_text: She names the short weight as a figure she will enter, not as a fault in the heat. He adjusts the counterweight, confirms the same number, and does not dispute it. She records the shortfall on the stock slate. They leave the bars on the pan long enough for the arm to hold.

She clears the forge balance of the last stock-check and sets a true bar on the pan. She watches the arm come level and does not look to him for confirmation. He sees the weighing and does not correct it. The true bar sits at the mark.

gr-01.beat_text: With the relic gone and no coin or fighters or replacement piece in the hamlet, the coming presentation and the year's grain-right stand at risk. The Hold's compact demands the relic with the iron. No watch is raised before morning.

She adds that she will work the winter because the hamlet cannot spare a smith, and that she will leave when the pass opens in spring. She does not ask him to approve the leaving. She does not withdraw it. He does not refuse the terms or treat them as a question.

No villager stands at the ground to hear a challenge or to be told one. Her frosted hands stay visible on the table edge while the steward closes the book. She lets the year's acceptance stand on a levy she will not name at the table. The steward leaves the accepted pieces on the board for the walk home.

gr-02.beat_text: The band withdraws the way they came, now holding the stolen presentation-piece among their poor kit. They do not post a claim or a message. They go because they are hungry, not because they mean to break a rite.

gr-03.beat_text: The steward names the year's protection and the grain-right as renewed, reading the compact as a record rather than a blessing. The steward releases them with the pass left open for the winter. The Hold's acceptance is the book-mark and nothing more. Willa does not correct the record.

cn-01.beat_text: He states that the original was lost in a slide year the village could not have survived, and that the reasons were good then. He names the hunger of that winter and the closed pass as the ground of the weld. He offers those reasons as history, not as a present plea. She lets him finish the account.

She does not break the piece. She does not take the reading to the village. She keeps both courses open long enough that neither can be finished cleanly before the steward's table. The object remains hers. What is owed cannot be settled in the days that remain.

When the last bar is stamped she restates the partition: silence now, winter labor, leaving at the spring opening. What is owed will not be cleared; it will be cut into costs each of them will carry. He does not bargain for a different cut. The house keeps working under those terms.

cn-02.beat_text: She keeps a count of days against the rite. By the time the far slope comes in sight the remaining days have fallen from twenty-one to fourteen. She does not rest an extra night to recover the spent strength.
She counts the remaining days against the presentation. By the time the home slope comes in sight the rite is six days off. She does not camp an extra night to spare the hands.

They stack the thin tithe by the door with the relic still in her keeping. Three days remain before the steward's table. She counts them against the walk to the midwinter ground, not against any further talk. He banks the fire. Neither reopens the terms.
